headlines.html: Europe warned of orbital compute gap: The European Space Policy Institute (ESPI) released a report warning that "Europe risks falling behind the United States and China in orbital data centers and becoming dependent on foreign infrastructure," recommending an EU-level flagship ODC program under its 2028–2034 research framework. — (SpaceNews)

California emerges as satellite mass-production hub: Despite cost and regulatory pressures, California has drawn one-third of U.S. space-tech companies and more than half of all space venture investment over the past five years to become a satellite mass-manufacturing hub, according to an analysis. Muon Space is running a 12,000-square-meter factory targeting 500 satellites a year. — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-06.summary_html:
① ESPI (SpaceNews, 8/5) — A report published by the European Space Policy Institute on August 5 warned that Europe could fall behind the United States and China in the orbital data center race and become dependent on foreign orbital compute infrastructure. The report identifies China as the frontrunner. In a coordinated push linking national policy, local governments, and state-owned enterprises, ADAspace's Three-Body Computing Constellation plans 2,800 satellites after launching 12 last May, while Shanghai's Xingshu Tiansuan network began deploying a 1,000-satellite fleet this July. In the United States, Starcloud and Cowboy Space are each attracting private capital at valuations exceeding $1 billion. Europe, by contrast, remains stuck in research and small-scale demonstrations — apart from the French startup Alatir, which is pursuing a robotically assembled ODC — with no large-scale deployment strategy, the report noted. ESPI recommended launching an EU flagship ODC program under the 2028–2034 research framework, having the EU and ESA serve as early customers, holding a "European ODC Challenge," and forming an international standards working group.

② California satellite manufacturing (SpaceNews, 8/5) — An industry analysis published the same day shows where the satellite mass-production base underpinning orbital data centers is concentrated. California is home to one-third of U.S. space-tech companies, more than half of all U.S. space venture investment over the past five years, and 10,000 aerospace engineers. Muon Space is targeting production of 500 satellites a year at a 12,000-square-meter factory, and the state is holding manufacturers in place with tax credits — $32.75 million for Vast, $24 million for Apex, and $12.7 million for True Anomaly. Among them is K2 Space, which is pursuing gigawatt-class satellite buses for orbital data centers. A mass-production base for communications and observation satellites is not itself an ODC, but since no orbital compute constellation is viable without cheap, high-volume satellites, this manufacturing density is the substance of the supply-chain advantage the United States holds. The two articles that appeared side by side on August 5 show two sides of the same axis — that the orbital data center race has now moved beyond the technology-demonstration stage into industrial and policy competition between nations. The ESPI report points to the policy vacuum: China is pushing hard as a state to seize standards, and U.S. venture capital is minting unicorns, while only Europe remains trapped in research with no coordinated deployment strategy. The California article shows, in concrete terms, where that U.S. advantage comes from — the manufacturing density that concentrates talent and capital in one place to churn out hundreds of satellites a year is the precondition for an ODC constellation. What Europe envies is exactly what California has: the policy gap and the industrial agglomeration are two faces of the same coin.

headlines.html: Spain commits up to €2 billion to IRIS² sovereign military satellite network: Spain has allocated up to €2 billion (about $2.3 billion) to build a national military satellite communications network tied into Europe's own IRIS² constellation, making it the largest single-nation backer — (SpaceNews)

U.S. Space Force awards K2 Space $22.9 million for satellite-to-satellite laser communications demo: K2 Space, which builds gigawatt-class buses for orbital data centers, has won a contract to demonstrate optical communications terminals that let satellites exchange data directly with one another — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-03.summary_html:
① Spanish Ministry of Defense (SpaceNews, 7/31) — Spain will invest between €1.6 billion and €2 billion in a national military satellite communications network to be integrated into IRIS², the European Union's low- and medium-Earth-orbit communications constellation. The figure surpasses the roughly $750 million pledged days earlier by Poland, making Spain the largest single-nation backer of IRIS². With a total program cost of €10.6 billion and a fleet of about 292 satellites, IRIS² is targeting full operation by 2030, and Spain will directly secure six medium-orbit and six low-orbit satellites along with a ground gateway station. The Ministry of Defense said the budget covers "the space segment, ground control, and the entire lifecycle of system operations." It is not an orbital data center in itself, but it reflects Europe's move to build sovereign infrastructure for mass-producing and operating satellites.

② K2 Space (SpaceNews, 8/1) — The U.S. Space Force is paying K2 Space $22.9 million to demonstrate satellite-to-satellite laser communications. K2 will procure, integrate, launch, and operate two of its own satellites fitted with the "Enterprise Space Terminal," with completion targeted for 2028. These optical terminals beam data directly between satellites without routing through a ground station, and they form part of the "space data network" the Department of Defense is pursuing to rapidly share missile-warning, tracking, and targeting information across a multi-orbit distributed surveillance layer. K2, which raised a $500 million Series D last week on the strength of its gigawatt-class large buses for orbital data centers, is with this optical demonstration validating the satellite-to-satellite optical backbone technology that any orbital compute constellation will require. Today's two stories are not about the "nodes" of an orbital data center but about the infrastructure and capital underpinning them. Spain's €2 billion speaks to who builds and owns the constellation — Europe's sovereignty over satellite mass production and operation — while K2's optical communications contract validates the optical backbone that carries data between satellites without a ground station. Neither is a data center in itself; both serve communications and defense. But mass-produced satellites and satellite-to-satellite optical networks are the precondition on which every orbital compute vision stands, whether SpaceX's million-satellite orbital data center or Starcloud's 88,000. While core headlines like Sophia Space's patents and regulatory debates take the front row, government and defense money is quietly flowing into the industrial base and optical backbone beneath them.

headlines.html: Orbital data center constellations need "rules of the road": As orbital data center plans on the scale of Starcloud's 88,000 satellites and SpaceX's 1 million take shape, a Washington policy panel warned that space traffic coordination standards to prevent satellite collisions must be established now — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-01.summary_html: ① SpaceNews (SpaceNews, 7/30) — At a July 29 panel hosted by the Secure World Foundation in Washington, Starcloud co-founder and chief technology officer Ezra Feilden, along with officials from The Aerospace Corporation, Planet, and the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Space Commerce, raised the question of traffic management for orbital data center constellations. Starcloud has filed for 88,000 satellites and SpaceX for as many as 1 million, and the analysis warns that satellite avoidance maneuvers — currently running in the hundreds of thousands per year — could surge to roughly 500 million per year in a 1-million-satellite era. The dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbits where data center satellites are expected to cluster are of particular concern, since every satellite must travel in the same direction; Feilden warned it would be "like a highway where no one has decided which lane to drive in — the risk of head-on collisions would be enormous." Participants proposed that industry set its own standards ahead of government-mandated regulation, through the Commerce Department's build-out of TraCSS, a space traffic coordination system modeled on air traffic control, and through the Space Commerce certification program, which is currently voluntary.
